chapter_theme: Three songs at Thirukkurangaduthurai (திருக்குரங்காடுதுறை), where monkeys play in the fields: a song only of Murugan's beauty and dance, a catalogue of courtesans who make ascetics falter, and the bent, staff-bound body in which the poet asks the feet even if he is born again.
structure_note: 879 is praise alone; 880 is a courtesan catalogue; 881 moves from women's glances to old age and rebirth.

879.reading: The poet asks whether he will tell of anything but the beauty of Murugan's crowned six faces, his earringed shoulders, the garlands and gems, the flaming vel, the red flower feet with anklets, and his dance each day to drum syllables. The praise names Rama, who sent the forest monkey into Ravana's grove to set fire and freed Sita, and who walked the great forest with bow and arrows, as the one to whom Murugan is dear, the hero whose vel ended the asuras' army, and the lord at Kurangaduthurai where cane mills hum in flowering groves.
879.nuance: The first half has no confession: it is a description of Murugan's form and dance (திமிந்தோதி திமித்திமி ... தினந்தோறு நடிப்பது), and the question புகல்வேனோ may mean 'shall I tell of it?' or 'shall I tell of anything else?'. The drum syllables are rhythm. கொடுந்தாரை வெயில் கயிலைத் தொடும் is obscure.

880.reading: The poet lists the women of scheming desire: singers, dancers who leap onto the stage, coaxers whose love falls short with anyone, who name a price of half a coin, with killing glances, nail-marked breasts and bitten lips, cheats who seek money every day, forms of sin who make ascetics falter, who melt men in pleasure, and asks whether he will give up the delusion of celebrating union with them. The praise names Murugan the bridegroom of the forest girl with dark scented hair, the great life of devotees like himself whom Indra and the gods remember, at Kurangaduthurai where the river's waves cast up the nine gems on the fields.
880.nuance: அரைப்பணம் கூறு விலையினர் and பொருட்டினம் தேடு கபடிகள் name the price and the greed. தவர் சோரப் புரித்திடும் பாவ சொருபிகள்: their power reaches even ascetics. நினைக்கும் என் போலும் அடியவர்: the poet counts himself among the devotees despite the confession.

881.reading: The poet speaks of women with pot-like breasts and garlands, caught in the net of their cool-faced glance, and then of the body bent and stooping, walking unsteadily, withered, never without its staff, sleeping and waking, being born and born again; even so, he asks, give the golden feet to wear on his chest. The praise names Vishnu who danced on the poisonous hoods, sleeps on the first serpent-bed, and broke his shackles and ran, the dark cloud, as uncle, and the lord of the shrine where peahens cry on the slopes, bees swarm, and monkeys leap in the fields.
881.nuance: பிறந்து பிறப்பேனும் ... பொற்பாதம் அருள்வாயே: the plea does not ask to end birth but for the feet even if he is born again. The move from the glance to the stooping body with its staff (கூனி, கோலும் அகலாதே) makes old age the sequel of desire. The Vishnu lines point to Krishna on Kaliya's hoods and his chains breaking at birth, but the reading of விலங்கை முறித்தோடி is mine.

links.note: Both picture the old man walking unsteadily on a staff after a life of desire; the Naladiyar says those still set on desire then have no way to safety, while 881 asks the golden feet even so, even if he is born again.

In 372, at Arunai, the poet asks not to spend day and night praising women in set comparisons but to be told by grace to think daily (அநுதினம் நினை) of Murugan's procession on the peacock. 879 does what 372 asks: it turns the same descriptive craft on Murugan's crowned six faces, shoulders, vel and anklets and his daily dance (தினந்தோறு நடிப்பது), and asks whether he would tell of anything else (புகல்வேனோ). The pairing shows the confession of 372 and its remedy, praise redirected to the god's form.

880 names women who quote a price (அரைப்பணம் கூறு விலையினர்), whose love falls short with anyone (குறைப்படுங் காதல் குனகிகள்) and who seek money every day (பொருட்டினந் தேடு கபடிகள்). Kural 911 says the sweet words of bangled women who desire wealth, not from love (அன்பின் விழையார் பொருள்விழையும்), bring harm. The song lists in detail the trade the Kural defines in one line: love absent, money sought.
